utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, do you wish us to play the other film, P78, also, a segment a little before and a little after the piece we were concentrating on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, please let us go back to film P78. That is the recording made by Djelo Jusic.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part do you want?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 19 minutes, 10 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is Stradun. You can see clearly how the slabs are perpendicular to the Stradun. Shall I freeze?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Play it unless I say otherwise. Your Honours, that was about 20 seconds of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, please look at the slabs. Look at this channel in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vilicic. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, we don't need the recording any more.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want the computer? Can I switch it off?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vilicic, just a few more brief questions. First of all, were you at Zarkovica on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I have been to Dubrovnik, but not to Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea at all what can be seen and what can't be seen from the Zarkovica locality?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume, but I cannot tell exactly what can be seen, what is visible. I had that photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us kindly, in relation to what you wanted to explain yesterday, but please, as briefly as possible and as concisely concerning the photograph mentioned in the Galic case, just a few sentences to explain the Honourable Chamber what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be grateful to the Trial Chamber, since I took off the Internet precisely the part of the transcript where I spoke about this case. There is a drawing where I clearly indicated the trajectory, the direction of descent of the projectile as indicated in the Prosecution material. There was a picture where I mistakenly turned by 180 degrees. It was never used for determining the direction, and I clearly said in my testimony on pages 2364, 63, 65, I clearly said when Honourable Judge Orie asked me that we did not rely on the picture for making our conclusions. We were strictly guided by the material provided and the direction was not changed anywhere. And I was astounded when I read in the Galic judgement in a footnote that Vilicic practically changed the direction of the projectile and indicated south-southeast instead of north. And I will kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to produce this part of the transcript because I emphatically said the direction does not change, and I never mentioned south or southeast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vilicic. Just tell us again on what pages of the transcript can we find this?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Transcript of the 27th February 2003 starting with page 20.363, 20.363, starting with line 17, up to the end, line 25, continuing on page 20.364, full page, and page 20.365, lines 1 to 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vilicic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if I could give the Trial Chamber this part of my testimony in transcript where one can clearly see what I exactly said about that wretched picture that was turned and the conclusion that was never changed relative to what was indicated in the Prosecution material, that the projectile came from the north, and our conclusion was that it was impossible to determine precisely from which precise location in the north it came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has access to this transcript. And if it deems necessary, they will review it. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender now the exhibits treated through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we finish with the evidence, though, Mr. Vilicic, I noted in the course of your evidence this morning that it was the conclusion that you reached in the course of your analysis that some 27 120-millimetre shells, mortar shells, and 106 82-millimetre mortar shells could have landed inside the Old Town when mortars were targeting targets outside the Old Town. Is that the basis -- have I correctly understood what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So altogether, you calculated or estimated 133 mortar shells might have landed?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In your report in the English-language version at page 89, or maybe page 4388 -- I think it's 89. There are two page references. 89, you have a -- it's in paragraph 6.4 --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- conclusion, and your conclusion number 11 which indicates that "if targeting had been carried out according to the prescribed norms, up to 81 120-millimetre shells and 206 82-millimetre shells with simple preparation of initial firing data, that is, a total of up to 287 shells, would have landed in the Old Town. And most of the features in the Old Town would have been completely destroyed." Firstly, on what basis do you form the view that if some 287 shells had landed in the Old Town, most of its features would have been completely destroyed? I'd like to understand that a little more.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We based that conclusion on the efficiency of 120-millimetre mortar shells and the effectiveness of 82-millimetre shells. Such a great number of 120-millimetre shells which have a greater destructive capacity than artillery, 120-millimetre shells, would have led to the destruction of a large number of facilities. Roofings, the whole buildings, frames, construction, all that would have been destroyed, demolished, and it would have been tragic for the town. Your Honour, this number of the regulation, of the standards, that indicates that if the town had been targeted according to the standard which is given in annex 17 indicating how many shells are needed to destroy a certain firing position, then we arrive at this number of shells. So our analysis was done for one combat kit in the report. In this alternative, we would have two to three combat kits per mortar which means that the mortars that were at Ledenice would have fired around 480 shells of 120 millimetres. If they had fired that, then at least 80 or more precisely 81 would have landed in the Old Town as a result of the dispersion we described in the report. And, Your Honours, that was our basis for concluding that the shooting was not carried out according to the standards for the destruction of these targets, that a significantly lower number of projectiles was fired, because if such a great number of projectiles had landed -- I'm sorry, you probably did not receive the revised version of this page. It is actually item 9, and in your copy it's item 11, point 2 is duplicated. And we see in two places points 2 and 3. Item 9, if targeting had been carried out according to the prescribed norms, up to 81 120-millimetre shells, et cetera ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In your process of analysis, I understand from what you're saying that you've taken into account what is prescribed in the JNA as to the amount of -- the number of shells that ought to be used to effectively destroy a particular target. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, what further interests me is the difference between your view that some 287 shells, of which some 81 were 120 millimetre, that they would have completely destroyed most of the features in the Old Town, and your view that the damage that we have seen and which you identified and used for the purposes of your report, the first two types of damage, that that could have been accomplished by 133 shells, of which 27 were 120 millimetre. The total number of mortar shells for total destruction is only just a little over double the number that you've used in the other proposition. Could you assist me there with that difference.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is double is the number that I indicated, 27. We concluded 27 shells of 120 millimetres would fall within the Old Town if one combat kit had been fired. In the other proposition, we assumed three combat kits that would have to have been fired to achieve this number. That is what the calculation shows. According to the standard, mortars would have had to fire 2.7 combat kits of 120 millimetres in order to destroy one source of fire, one firing position. So this number is three times higher than the conclusion that we arrived at, assuming one combat kit. We said that one combat kit is 27 shells of 120 millimetres, and if the standard had been followed there would have been 81 shells. That is the calculation that led us to this correlation, 27 as opposed to 81. We were following the number of shells that would have had to be fired according to the standard indicated in Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond annex 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My question was attempting to focus on the difference between the damage that was actually caused according to the report which you acted on for the 133 shells and your view that the Old Town, or most of its features, would have been completely destroyed by just some 287 shells. Is that a reliable view?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, honestly, this is just an estimate. But the number before, 27 and 106 is consistent with the first and second grade damaged buildings. I'm referring to the damage that was caused because we have between 8 and 12 of the first and second grade, and around 72 of the second grade, second category of damage. If we start out with the assumption that it would have to have been direct impacts to cause that sort of damage. And the third and fourth grade damage is usually damage to the walls, doors, or windows. Those are not direct impacts, but rather indirect ones, which means that a shell fell somewhere near the building, closer to it or further away from it. It was based on that correlation that we reached our conclusion, and the number of impacts that landed as a result of the targeting of positions outside the Old Town is more or less the same as the number of features that were destroyed, or rather reported as having been destroyed inside the Old Town, not the exact number, but, as I said, this was the second time we used this information on the number of damaged buildings inside the Old Town. So we have about 90 features or buildings which is consistent with between 90 and a hundred-and-something shells that was fired, 108, specifically I believe. In the first analysis, the number was 106 82-millimetre shells, a total of 106, and 27 120-millimetre shells as well as 82, 79, a total of 106 shells. So that was the conclusion, conclusion number 10 in your document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very roughly speaking, you're concluding that one combat pack could have caused the damage that has been identified in the report, and that roughly three combat packs would be necessary to completely destroy most of the features in the Old Town. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There would be a lot more damage to the Old Town. In terms of some kind of symmetry, certainly twice or three times as great in terms of how many buildings would be damaged, and I'm referring to the first and second degree of damage or category of damage. Your Honour, if I may allow, that is precisely why our conclusion was, the conclusion based in our report, that the targeting was not deliberate because there is consistency between the fired projectiles against external targets, targets outside the Old Town. There was consistency with the number of damaged buildings of the first and second category inside the Old Town, and that was the only basis that we had for that conclusion. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it you proceeded on the assumption that the damage is all caused by mortar shells. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of the damage was caused by mortar shells. When I reviewed the footage, I saw two 120-millimetre projectiles that failed to actually explode. I listened to witness testimonies as I was following this trial, and most of the Prosecution witnesses mentioned that they had found the stabilisers and that they kept them as keepsakes. The exact number of shells, the only way to ascertain the exact number of shells and I'm rather surprised that this was not done by the Croatian side is if you collect all these stabilisers, because the stabilisers are left behind, 120-millimetre shell stabilisers that should have been shown to this Honourable Trial Chamber in order to say which exact number of shells landed inside the Old Town. It really very much surprises me that the police seem to have been unable for the purpose of this case to collect the number of those shells and to present the Honourable Trial Chamber with the exact number, or rather the stabilisers. That would have constituted some very specific proof that indeed such-and-such number of shells did land inside the Old Town. But nothing short of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've proceeded on the basis of reading the testimony of witnesses and looking at the video evidence to reach your assumption that most of the damage was due to mortars. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And also, in our report we mentioned that we did not mention any damage caused by the small-calibre navy weapons, 20 millimetre, 40 millimetre, and 57-millimetre weapons. Bearing in mind the angle of the trajectory, the only thing that could have been damaged inside the Old Town were the roofs because those were flat trajectories and not curved ones as in mortars. Therefore, there would have been no chance for those projectiles to land inside the Old Town to begin with. So the most damage that could have been caused, we saw the external damage, and we wrote that from the sea, there was no footage that was taken from the sea for us to see whether the external walls of the Old Town sustained any damage. The only damage to the outer part of the walls, as I said, was caused by the engine of a Maljutka rocket. It remained lodged inside the wall of the Old Town once the damage had been caused. But that was the only thing we could notice in that particular footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I correctly understand it to be your view that smaller naval weapons could have mostly hit roofs in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And going back to what you were trying to say to Mr. Weiner, some of the language in your report could suggest otherwise, but is it really that we should understand that you are proceeding on the basis that all JNA firing was targeted at suspected or known Croatian weapon sites outside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I also mentioned that the C-6 position at 500 metres from the Old Town was the only one we chose ourselves, whereas the other position that was at a hundred metres from the Old Town is consistent with the anti-aircraft gun. I saw that in Jozo Poje's document. And you remember, Your Honours, I was here for his testimony, and there was that discussion about the angle or the rear and the frontal gradient in relation to that particular gun, that was when we introduced in our analysis also the position of this particular gun. It was based on Ivan Negodic's testimony that we introduced C-4, which was another position about 200 metres to the east of the Old Town. And we took from General Nojko Marinovic the Bogosica Park position because he stated categorically twice that two 82-millimetre mortars and one 120-millimetre mortar was placed there which I was quite surprised to hear, if I may say, because Negodic categorically denied that. And Zoran Primic, in his report, said he was the commander of that unit until as late as June 1992. It would have been highly unlikely on such a day, at such a decisive moment for the Defence of Dubrovnik town that at least two key mortar positions, I'm talking about the one 200 metres away from the gate of Ploce and the one in Bogosica Park were silent, or not operating if you like, while an attack was being carried out from Bosanka. Firing position were there that could target Bosanka and that could prevent their fire and prevent the attack that was coming on from the flank, from the direction of Zarkovica and Bosanka, and against Srdj. However, as I've already said, we drafted this expert analysis for you to use as a document which could help you to compare the real situation with witness statements. And if then the conclusion that this or that was what really happened, then what follows from that or based on that is precisely what we stated in our expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That has helped us, Mr. Vilicic. I'm happy to tell you that your evidence is now at an end, and you are now able to return to your other work. So may we thank you for your assistance here in this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours, for giving me a chance to testify before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I would like to have documents related to Mr. Vilicic's testimony admitted into evidence. We believe that the conditions have been met for their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was an objection when it was tendered at the evidence in chief, Mr. Weiner. Is that maintained now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to say any sections, conclusions or inferences that are not based on the evidence should either be excluded, or at least given less weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you can rely on the last part. And I raise that very point at the beginning. But I think in fairness to the witness to understand his evidence, we really need the whole of the report because it discloses on what basis various conclusions were reached. And as he has just finished saying, if those conclusions aren't ones which are supported by the evidence, well obviously the conclusion has no foundation. I think, Mr. Petrovic, we've managed to dispose of Mr. Weiner's objection, and we would receive the full report. That will be received as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be D115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there were also placed before us two sheets of paper to do with the trajectories and targeting. Are you wanting those as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. May those two also be admitted as Defence exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the curriculum vitae of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would like to tender that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems to be the extent of the documentary exhibits concerning the evidence of the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope so. And I hope that when you decided to receive the expert report, your decision also included the annexes to the expert report, annex 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I said the full report, intending by that to include the annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. I apologise if I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has no further witnesses that it wishes to bring before this Trial Chamber. In relation to the last witness that was envisaged, according to the plan and to the 62 ter list that we provided, the Defence has already notified the parties in writing, and we would like to do it orally now, too. We have withdrawn the expert report and no longer wish this expert to testify before this Chamber. Therefore, this brings the Defence case to an end. We have two exceptions, however: Two expert reports, medical expert reports by an orthopedic expert and something else that was submitted pursuant to Rule 94 bis, a urologist's report, the OTP did not request that those two witnesses be called in for cross-examination. So pursuant to Rule 95 bis, I would propose that the Trial Chamber make a ruling in order to receive these two reports as Defence exhibits, specifically I'm referring to Dr. Micic's report and to Dr. Vuckovic's report. Both were submitted on the 22nd of June this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The orthopedic report, is that Dr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Dr. Vuckovic's report is the orthopedic one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, they're both tendered with relevance to mitigation, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. With relevance to that only, as has been confirmed by the Defence team in writing to our learned friends from the OTP and to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dr. Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- will be D118. And the second report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- will be D119.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was today that the Defence has filed a motion, [In English] "Proposed Defence Exhibits into evidence," which is a motion in which a certain number of documents that were part of the 65 ter Defence list are being proposed for admission into evidence as Defence exhibits. I'm not sure if the motion has reached you, Your Honour. But in that motion, we have provided an elaborate explanation as to the substance of each and every one of those documents - thank you - as well as the reasons why, pursuant to Rule 89, these exhibits should be received into evidence as Defence exhibits. It is our position that these exhibits meet all the necessary requirements for being admitted as Defence exhibits. The motion was filed just this morning, and I expect that my learned friends and colleagues will soon be in a position to take a position in relation to that motion, following which the Trial Chamber will be able to make a ruling on our motion. We also sincerely hope that the proposed exhibits will be received as Defence exhibits as a result of that ruling. Your Honours, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The motion has been received, but only this morning. I really can say that no member of the Chamber has had a chance to look at it yet. But we will see what is the position of the Prosecution on it. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I look across the sea of faces wondering who it is going to speak these days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is I for now. Thank you very much. We have indeed received only this morning both news of the withdrawal of the expert and the pile of exhibits that Mr. Petrovic has just made reference to. We will speedily look at those and have a response so that there's no untoward delay for the Chamber. The -- there was another issue I think that the Chamber had raised, and if we're finished with this particular point, I would ask for leave to address it whenever the Chamber would permit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position, then, in respect of the motion of today's date of the Defence for the reception of a number of documents as exhibits will be necessarily deferred to allow the Prosecution to respond. I take it the parties would expect the Chamber to deal with it on the basis of the written motion and the written response.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As the Chamber did with ours, as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There will be no need for a further hearing just for that. Very well. And subject to that, I take it the case for the Defence is closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First of all to you, to my colleagues, thank you for your attention and your patience over the past 19 days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We have been impressed that there has been such attention, if I might say so, to the need to deal with matters expeditiously. And we are grateful for that. One matter the Chamber would mention, there has been a number of references in the evidence to sunrise and nightfall, sunset. There has been no specific evidence. It's a matter that could be taken into account Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond as a matter of judicial knowledge. It's a matter that turns essentially on matters of objective geography and the like and statistical data is available. And I believe the Chamber's legal officer has placed one possible source of that in the hands of both Prosecution and Defence counsel to see if they are content that the Chamber might accept that as a proper indication of the times in Dubrovnik of sunrise and sunset and the like on the 6th of December 1991. Do you have any view on that, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had an opportunity to see the document. We cannot check it, but we do believe, nevertheless, that it had been acquired from reliable sources and that therefore it can serve as a basis for the Honourable Chamber for making judgement and conclusions pertaining to this area as necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It indicates, if I could record it, that the beginning of civil twilight on Friday, the 6th of December 1991 was 0631, and sunrise was at 0703 hours; that sunset was at 1614 hours, and that the end of civil twilight was 1646 hours. There is also information on the moon's transition. Ms. Somers, do you have any view on this information and the proposition that it might be accepted by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for presenting it. This is the first I've seen it, Your Honour. In principle, the source certainly looks to be a reliable source. And I have no immediate objection. I would be interested actually to see if there is a similar source that exists in the region. But this does look like it certainly would be a valuable basis for the Chamber to proceed upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The source I might add is that magical thing called the Internet, so if there is some other basis --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the source that the Internet refers to looks certainly to be a reliable one. I believe there do exist as well a region similar types of observation centres. And if we are able to find an additional one, we'll certainly notify the Chamber and Defence, if the Chamber will permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I have just been reminded that we have a number of Defence documents which are marked for identification but not yet exhibited. I might list them in the transcript; and if the parties would give a very short written submission on them, because I assume you may not at the moment have them immediately in your mind, either party, a short written submission in the next three days or so as to the admissibility of each. I'll list them as I understand them to be, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: D13, D14, D15, D16, D18, D30, D63, D72, D73, and D74. Now, I've got to say I don't remember and can't vouch for each of those, but they seem to be documents at the moment that are still only marked for identification. So there are quite a few of them, and it would be important to get them clarified as to whether or not they should be received in evidence. A number of photographs were the first ones, newspaper articles, minutes of sessions of the Government of Montenegro, et cetera. So a number of documents to be looked at by both parties in a short written submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we shall give our response as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Subject to that, those questions yet to be resolved about admissibility of evidence, the Defence case is closed. Now, Ms. Somers, there was a further matter then that you foreshadowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is the issue of rebuttal. And I wish to ask the Chamber's leave to have until later this afternoon to indicate whether or not the Prosecution will indeed bring a rebuttal witness. I would be grateful for it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That witness could be heard tomorrow, perhaps a little later in the morning if you did decide. Would that be convenient?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It may. It does not depend necessarily on me. It is a logistical issue as well, as the Chamber may know. So if it is not possible, only because we had worked on a completely different schedule, as I'm sure you're aware. If, for any reason, it is not, then we would ask simply for first thing, if it's possible, Monday. And no later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The second thing, Monday, we're listed at 2.15 in the afternoon, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No later than Monday, brief, extremely narrow, and hopefully very quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be preferable from the point of view of the Defence team if it were possible tomorrow. It would then free up the Defence team to attend to other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask the Chamber what would be the latest tomorrow, if in fact -- is there a possibility if logistically it is difficult for reasons beyond our control, is there an afternoon possibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are listed for tomorrow morning. And can I say that I have a commitment in the early afternoon. So if I'm right in guessing who might be the witness, it would be confined to two short issues, the evidence, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There would be some perhaps cross-examination on those two matters. I would think it may be possible between as late as midday tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Starting as late as midday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to express my concern and skepticism that this is feasible to happen tomorrow given the fact that we don't know who the witness would be and could be, and what the testimony would be about. So if I received this information during this afternoon, and if we get it late in the afternoon, I don't believe that we can do the cross-examinations efficiently tomorrow because we cannot even guess who the person in question is and to what circumstances the person is going to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let me say, Mr. Petrovic, that I have proceeded on the assumption that the witness will be Admiral Jokic and that he will be called to deal with the two particular matters which the Chamber has already indicated the Prosecution could have leave to call him about by way of rebuttal. And it's on that basis that I have assumed that he might be available tomorrow and that his evidence will be of short duration and any cross-examination will be of short duration. And I think that you would be well aware of and familiar with those issues. If it's some other witness and some other issues, I would entirely accept what you're putting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That was very helpful for the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one more matter, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It would be an oral motion solely by the Prosecution, it is not a joint motion. There had been discussion of a site visit. And although I realise there are always logistical issues, should the Chamber find that it is logistically feasible, the Prosecution supports and would file a subsequent written submission, supports the idea of a site, as it were, crime-scene visit and location visit. It is not -- it would not be the first time it has been done in this institution. I think it would be very beneficial. And it is subject, as I understand it, to all practical and logistical considerations, but we will submit this within the next 24 hours. I just wanted to make sure the Chamber knew our position on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Ms. Somers. You will readily appreciate that it is not an easy matter to arrange. It takes judicial time and other time to accommodate. It is not a cheap exercise. And it would be undertaken if the Chamber were persuaded that it really would be of material assistance in determining a range of factual matters that are in dispute in this case. But we would certainly like to hear the Defence position about that. What would be contemplated, of course, is a view of the Dubrovnik and some of the particular localities that have featured in the evidence and the immediate surroundings of Dubrovnik. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, fully aware of all the problems and difficulties implied in this context, and the time necessary and high cost, the Defence quite simply would like to leave this entirely up to you to decide. If the Honourable Chamber believes that this will contribute to clarifying certain issues, the Defence will, of course as we did so far, honour your decision be it as it may. But at this point in time, the Defence cannot say now whether it is necessary or not. We leave it up to you to decide whether this is necessary to shed more light on the circumstances surrounding this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If there were to be a view or a site visit, it clearly should precede final oral submissions by the parties so that the final oral submissions could take account of the view. And it would be important for at least one counsel from both the Defence and Prosecution teams to be with the Trial Chamber for the visit for obvious reasons. And it would be important for each team to have a list of matters which each team considers should be viewed by the Trial Chamber so that we could be sure in the visit of seeing all matters considered important to view by both sides. I foreshadow those matters so that people would understand how we would approach the matter. That brings me to another issue which is of interest. Clearly we may not assemble now as a Chamber unless the Prosecution is to call rebuttal evidence. We may not assemble again as a Chamber to hear any further evidence. And so we could look at the question of forward planning on that basis. When this matter was last discussed, both Prosecution and Defence were concerned that more time would be valuable for the preparation of final written submissions. And with that in mind, the Chamber would be prepared to extend the time that it had foreshadowed for written submissions to be filed no later than Monday, the 30th of August, which is a week later than was earlier planned. And that will be the order of the Trial Chamber. If there were to be an inspection, it may well be one that could then be accommodated during that week, the week commencing Monday, the 30th of August. If that were the case, final oral submissions could be taken sometime during the week following. Now, in fairness to everybody not on the Monday, but probably on the Wednesday and Thursday, the 8th and 9th of September. As indicated earlier, given the extent of written submissions, to allow the possibility of a day's submissions from each side would appear to be an adequate provision. So they would then be the plans of the Trial Chamber at the present time. While it is unfortunate that the August break comes now, on this plan the accused should not be disadvantaged because the time, I'm afraid, the Chamber has imposed on counsel to prepare their final written submissions. So we would hope that the delay will be no longer because of the vacation. And we can then move as quickly as possible after that. Now, with respect to a view, we will receive your motion when it is filed, Ms. Somers, and we will make an analysis of the issues and the importance. And in view of what has been said by counsel, come to a decision quickly, and you will be advised by our legal officer whether there will be one. And that will be done quickly so that it will be possible to make the necessary arrangements. And as I've indicated, that ought to follow as quickly as possible after the receipt of the final written submissions as we can manage. Probably two or perhaps three days would be the time to be allocated to the view. It's not altogether clear to me yet how many sites would need to be visited and what time would be necessary. But allow, I would think, up to three days for that. And can I make it clear, there is yet to be a decision whether it is necessary and whether it can be arranged. So don't go off on the basis that there is to be one; we're merely looking ahead at that contingent possibility. Are there any further matters that should be raised at this time? If not, we will await your communication, Ms. Somers, on the matter of evidence with the strong encouragement to it being arranged for tomorrow if the Chamber's anticipation of who the witness might be is correct. And if so, it could be arranged to commence at noon, the middle of the day. We will await your written motion on the question of a view. We will await the parties' written submissions on the matters of evidence that remain outstanding and we will deal with those in due course. And we will communicate our decision with respect to a view as soon as we come to it. It remains to thank counsel for their assistance that we have had to this time and the increasing spirit of concern and cooperation that the proceedings could be concluded in as quick a time as reasonable so as to avoid any unnecessary further delay and anxiety for the accused, and frankly any unnecessary loss and waste of time for all of us. The Chamber will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
